title: Closing Sesshin Reflection
speaker: Myoki Raizelah Bayen
summary: The talk's main teaching emphasizes the importance of transcending dualities and conceptual thinking in Zen practice, encouraging listeners to open their minds and experience the present moment as it truly is. By letting go of intellectual understanding and embracing embodiment, practitioners can manifest their true nature through action and presence, aligning with Dogen Zenji's teachings on the Genjokoan. This approach recognizes that awakening and bodhisattva nature are already present within all beings, and invites individuals to embody this reality without striving or attachment.
topics: Dogen's teachings on the nature of reality

sentences.text: How nice that we got to chant that all together for the last eight weeks.
I've been chanting it by myself and with you on Zoom, but now I get to hear your voices, and how lovely.
I want to start by welcoming our friends that are Zooming in: Kate and Jeff, welcome, and Kim, and Toy, and Karen, and Chris Blake, and Ray.
Thanks for joining us.
I see that I'm backlit.
I don't know if there's anything to be done about it, but here we all are.
How nice.
There are so many ways I could start this talk, but I want to start by acknowledging both the absence and the presence of our Dharma friend, Edie Norton.
I keep seeing her there in my mind's eye.
For the last year and a half, since I was practicing being Ino, I would sit there and she would sit behind me, and I could feel her presence and her steadfast practice.
Her steadfast practice lasted until the day she died on her hospice bed.
She's no longer with us physically, but she lives in the heart of so many people here.
I know much longer than I've been here, she practiced with Red Cedar for over 20 years.

She was ordained as a priestess here at Red Cedar, and she contributed to the Sangha in so many ways, including serving on the board, and she supported many people as a mentor, as a guide and as a teacher.
She left us with a precious gift, this book that has her Dharma name, Autumn Light.
It's not just about her life, but primarily about her experience at Tassajara during practice period, and I want to share some words from her book.
It's written into my talk, that's why I put the book down.
So this is from Edie.
*Zazen is a window into the unconscious.
It informs us about emotions, beliefs, perspectives we didn't know we had.
What comes up during Zazen can be disturbing or alarming, but it helps us to know ourselves in deeper ways than before.
Sometimes in Zazen, we encounter difficult emotional material we'd rather avoid.
We might be tempted to stop sitting or to leave.
This is when sitting with a group is helpful.
Maybe we feel obliged not to disturb them, so we stick it out and observe what happens next.
Not giving up.*
I mistyped something.
My volume?
Okay.
I wish I had written down the page.
*Not giving up trains the mind to be steadfast.
Sitting with others encourages dedication and right effort.
We learn that everyone's effort helps everyone in practice.
We learn that everyone's effort helps everyone in practice.*
Edie's talking about the importance of sangha.
This is one of our three treasures, one of our three refuges.
I take refuge in Buddha.
I take refuge in Dharma.
And I take refuge in sangha.
I appreciate the attention she brings here to sangha.
This practice period has brought the importance of sangha even more into focus for me.
I feel tremendous gratitude for this sangha in particular, for all of you and your continued support.

As I venture into the practice of Shuso for these recent months, I feel gratitude for my teachers and all the Buddhas and ancestors who, through innumerable conditions, somehow brought us all together here in this basement room of [unclear: "Buff"] in the northwest corner of the United States, so far away across the oceans from China and then Japan, from which this practice came.
How did that happen?
What a miracle.
I want to take a few minutes here to express my gratitude.
First, to my teacher.
I am so grateful for Chris, who has met with me regularly over the months leading up to practice period and throughout practice period.
She shared her undying commitment to practice, her continued support, her open heart, and her laughter.
You are truly a beacon of light, Chris.
Thank you for being here now and always gently guiding me, accepting me, and offering your support during both the joys and the challenges you've watched me go through in my life.
And I'm grateful to other teachers who have supported my practice over the years, Norman Fischer, Reb Anderson, and countless other teachers who have touched me through practice and their sharing.
Thank you to those who have guided me in the exploration of the Genjokoan, such as Okumura, Judith Regier, and so many others.

Thank you to the teachers who have come before us, Suzuki Roshi, Uchiyama, and of course Dogen, and to all the teachers who came before their teachers and their teachers, all the way back to Shakyamuni Buddha.
I also want to thank my husband, whose love is an unshakable pillar of support in my life and in my practice.
And I want to thank my benji, Ken, who has stood by my side these months managing tech and logistics.
Thank you.
And so much gratitude to all of you, to the Sangha.
Without you I would have no one to practice being Shuso with.
And in the last year and a half I would have had no one to practice being Ino with.
I need you.
I can't practice these roles without you.
And to me these roles, all the Zen-Do roles, including being Tenkan and Jisha and so on and so forth, they're so important because they give us an opportunity to meet ourselves, to study.
Not only have you given me the opportunity to study myself, to meet myself, and we know what Dogen says next: forget the self.
Thank you to all of you for providing a container for me to practice in, and for practicing alongside me and for journeying with me through the Genjokoan.
I actually asked Desiree to invite the service this morning, morning service C, that included the Genjokoan, because we're not quite done with practice period or the Genjokoan.
Maybe it will never be done.
But there's actually more that could be said.
Maybe for you it was a challenging text.
Many people find Dogen frustrating.
I've even heard the word infuriating used to describe him.
Some people, and I can remember, in my early years just going, huh?
Feeling this incomprehensibleness.
Dogen's thought and speech don't match our linear conceptual frame of minds.
In fact, the way he writes Genjokoan is more circular than linear.
He starts out making his point in the first three lines and then he circles back time and time again.
Can you hear me now?
Is my volume okay?
So let's go back to the beginning.
*All things are Buddha Dharma.
There is delusion and realization, practice, birth and death, and there are Buddhas and sentient beings.
As the myriad things are without an abiding self, there is no delusion, no realization, no Buddha, no sentient being, no birth and death.
The Buddha way is basically leaping clear of the many and the one.*
Could you hear that?
Okay, just wanted to make sure over the vacuum cleaner.
So there's duality, right?
There is delusion and realization, birth and death, Buddhas and sentient beings, and because of that, there's practice.
At the same time, we're empty of separate selves.

Boundarylessness, boundlessness, the boundless, spacious aspect of our being and the relative world: this is what Dogen is referring to in the second line, and then the Buddha way is basically leaping clear of both, the two and the one.
So Dogen rephrases this message in so many ways throughout, with metaphors, stories, poetry, and in the end, the story of Zen Master Baoche, which we would call a koan.
Dogen circles back several times.
It's right here.
It's right now.
When we show up fully, we wake up to both the delusion of enlightenment and the enlightenment of delusion.
Not two, not one.
Some call this the fundamental point, others may call it the frustrating point.
We just can't learn this through academic study.
Our minds simply aren't up for the task.
Judith Regier, in her essay in Receiving the Marrow, told us:
*Dogen can be relied upon to try to trick our brain through his semantics and the changing of syntax, in showing all the angles and contradicting all the opposite.
He dismantles our notions of solidity.
He encouraged us to open our minds beyond concepts and experience just this moment as it's realized.
Open our minds beyond concepts and experience just this moment as it's realized.*
The person that compiled the essays in this book, Teachings on Dogen by Soto Zen Women Priests, the editor is Frances Carney.
She adds:
*Dogen believed that language itself was a tool to open and liberate us.

Thus, as a linguist, he had the ability to play with language poetically, to nudge the mind beyond the intellect as to soak in the very water that reflects the moon in order to move us to the experience of awakening.
To nudge the mind beyond the intellect as to soak in the very water that reflects the moon.*
We all want to get it, right?
We all want to get what Dogen is saying.
So how do we get out of the way?
Let's just pause and take a conscious breath, feeling your belly expand with the breath and then empty.
This is why we're here at sesshin, to drop our awareness into our body, to settle.
Remember the An in Genjokoan, to massage, to knead, or to press.
I really like that, so I'm coming back to it.
And I'm actually going to invite us to do a little bit of self-massage.
I'll guide you through a little bit of facial self-massage.
So start out just by bringing the warmth of your hand to your face and then brushing through your face.
Brushing across the forehead, the cheeks, the jaw.
You can include the scalp, the ears.
Just feel the sensation of your hand against your skin or your hair.
Let's do it with the finger pads of our index finger and our thumb.
Let's start at the inner brow and squeeze across the brow, gradually moving from the inner brow out.
Just noticing again the sensation now of squeezing, maybe a little different than brushing.
And then bring a couple fingers right into your temple and make circles.
Maybe a different sensation with a different touch.
I'm bringing your fingers starting right where your outer nostril meets your face and then use a finger or two to gently press up under the cheekbone, moving out towards the ear.
And then when you get in front of the ear, I'll tell you a secret.
It's not really a secret.
Where the top of the ear meets the face and where the ear flap meets the face and where the ear lobe meets the face, there are some nice acupressure points that help to release the jaw.
So what feels good?
Pressing with your fingers, circling.
Sometimes I like to take the whole index finger and press and then let the rest of my hand fall onto my cheek.
What's that like?
Squeezing the whole face between your two palms.
And then come to the jaw and we can do the same thing we did at the eyebrow.
Squeezing between your finger pads and your thumb pad, moving out towards the ear.
And this big muscle here, the masseter, it attaches all the way up at the hairline.
So you can massage the masseter muscle.
That's what helps you chew.
Coming all the way up through the temple and the forehead.
And then just end by brushing through your face again.
And brush through your scalp, down onto your shoulders, the back of your neck.
Brush down your arms.
And then just take a moment to notice sensations.
How does it feel to be in your body?
Did doing this help you to actualize the point, to settle right here?
Does it support you in massaging to show up more fully, to enter this moment?
In Fukanzazengi, Dogen instructs us:
*You should therefore cease from practice based on intellectual understanding, pursuing words and following after speech.
And learn the backward step that turns your light inward to illuminate the self.
Body and mind will drop away from themselves and your original face will manifest.*
Cease from practice based on intellectual understanding.
Learn the backward step that turns your light inward to illuminate the self.
Study the self.
Study your experience.
Be with what emerges fully.
Be yourself fully.
Body and mind will drop away.
Your self-clinging will fall away.
Your ideas about yourself, the identities you hold onto, your notions of who you should be, eventually drop away.
I find when I study the self, these ideas, these identities, they start to soften.
The grip on my consciousness starts to loosen.
And then he says, your original face will manifest.
Your Buddha nature will manifest itself.
Notice again the word manifest.
This comes up a lot in the Genjokoan.
It caught my attention, so I looked it up in the dictionary for a precise definition: *to display or show by one's acts, to demonstrate.* To me, demonstrate also implies action.
And Okumura said something, in fact, about this at the very beginning of his book on the Genjokoan.
I'm quoting Okumura now:
*When we study and practice according to Dogen Zenji's teaching, it is important that we use more than our intellectual understanding of these views.*
I'm going to say that again.
*It is important that we use more than our intellectual understanding of these views or aspects of reality.
We actually should manifest these views with our actions.*
More than our intellectual understanding, we actually should manifest these views with actions.
Live it, he's saying.
Embody it.
Express it through your actions.
A few mornings ago, it was raining outside, so I decided to skip my morning walk and instead hopped onto the stationary bike in our basement.
And while I was riding it, I turned on a Dharma talk by Okumura called Introduction to Zen.
I thought it might be a good way to keep beginner's mind alive.
I think he was talking to a group of Tibetan Buddhists and he was describing our particular meditation practice, Shikantaza.
He translates Shikantaza as just sitting.
Zazen, on the other hand, is translated as sitting meditation.
Meditation, he explains, is something you do with the mind.
Sitting is something we do with the body.
Dogen emphasized just sitting, Shikantaza, being with posture and with breath.
I was taught in my early years at Green Gulch to pay attention to the movement of the breath in the belly, to follow the breath right down here into the hara.
Zazen is a body practice.
Yes, we're aware of our mind when we sit.
Thoughts, stories, conversations arise, but the practice is to let go and return to just sitting.
Posture and breath.
Return to the body.
But sitting doesn't just happen on the cushion.
Dogen says that it happens when we're lying down, when we're walking, in all of our daily activities.
So when we stand up at the end of sesshin and take our sitting practice with us out into the world, into your daily activities, this is what I believe Dogen is talking about: living the teaching.
We've been, all of us, raised in a culture that values and supports residing in our heads.
Most of us, and myself included, tend to live our lives leading with our heads.
But what is it like to lead with the body?
The body, the breath, the posture.
To fully inhabit these bodies.
My teacher calls it Zazen body.
How do you bring Zazen body into your daily life?
Into everything you do.
Your relationships, your household tasks, your work.
These are the questions that guide my life.
So we've spent two months, two precious months together, exploring the Genjokoan.
I think most of you here were in the class.
Here are a few translations of Genjokoan: *To actualize the fundamental point.
The ordinary profundity of the present moment becoming the present moment.
Realizing reality as it is.
To show up fully.* The Genjokoan is a koan to live by for the rest of our lives.
I didn't know this when I chose the Genjokoan as our topic of study, but I understand now why so many Dogen scholars consider this text to be Dogen's central teaching or offering.
Thus it's at the heart of our tradition.
Practicing as Shuso, I was sitting in, quote, the teacher's seat.
Genjokoan is not something I can teach you.
The way I see it, we were all simmering in the stew of the Genjokoan together.
I believe the Genjokoan is something we each need to discover for ourselves.
That's why I called the class Discovering Your Genjokoan.
And each of you did discover your own, which is all of ours.
And we discovered as a group.
I want to share what we discovered as a group.
I created a new poem bringing together lines from the poems that you all wrote at the end of the last class.
So everybody's words are included.
*Allow, relax, show up, forgetting the self, making the two one.
Unperturbable, each moment is unique.
Delusion and enlightenment is a public display of affection.
That is without knowledge, only knowing.
Into this placeless place.
The Buddha way is way beyond me.
Connected to all things.
Our view can be clouded.
Notice no self.
Actualize love and compassion for all beings.
This is the vital path of awakening.
Join the group.
All we have is right now.
Practice happens in each moment.
Everything interconnected.
Daily life offers awakening, bodhisattvas everywhere.
The light shines in all beings.
Buddha nature, arising, no chasing, fish and sea, bird and sky.
Why are you trying to be when you already are?
The practice is in your bones.
No obstacles, open hand.
Faith, practice, life awakened now is unique.
Owning a place on the path in the moonlight.
I am the little dewdrop, small and inconspicuous, yet brilliant on the green leaf.
Realizing that this has always been my journey.*
That's so beautiful.
None of those words were my own.
Thank you so much for walking this path with me.
For exploring together.
For simmering in the pot with me.
And I know that, yes, in linear time, practice period is ending, but it also never ends.
And we get to continue to practice together in this tiny corner up in the Northwest United States.
We somehow all found each other in the basement of [unclear: "Buff"].
What a miracle.
I have one more poem I'd like to share.
This one was written by our dear friend Okumura, who has helped me, and I hope each of you, so much in the exploration we shared.
This is Okumura's poem about the Genjokoan.
*All of us are always living in the present moment, the profundity of the present moment.
Even when we don't know it, and are blind to it, the profundity of the present moment is embracing us as the present moment.
All of us are living out the self interpenetrating whole world, the profundity of the self interpenetrating whole world, whether we know it or not.
Even when we doubt it and reject it, still, we are the self interpenetrating whole world, including delusions and doubts.
This is the present moment of the self interpenetrating whole world fanning the wind of profundity of life right now.
And right here is Genjokoan, the ordinary profundity of the present moment becoming the present moment.*
We are given this life to wake up in.
What a blessing.
Thank you, everyone.
*Dharma leads us into them.
Buddha's ways unsurpassable.
I vow to become*
